accepted.trend: UPI MDR For Capital Markets: Why A Tiny Fee Could Test India’s Zero-brokerage Model
accepted.context: Urban 30-year-olds grew up on the promise of the internet being free, but are now paying subscriptions for basic existence.
accepted.angle: The illusion of the modern, zero-fee digital India was actually just the pre-heating cycle of the oven.
slides: Remember 2017 when everything on your phone was free?

Then: Zero brokerage. Zero fee. Unlimited data.
Now: Platforms charge ₹5 to pay bills. Apps charge ₹10 to exist. UPI wants a cut of your investments.

The trial period of your adulthood has expired.

Please enter your card details.
accepted.caption: Your free trials have ended. Please pay to continue breathing.

accepted.context: Young parents are overwhelmed by the hyper-convenience economy where children's basic needs are treated as emergency deliveries.

10-minute delivery of diapers: ₹800.
Organic pureed apple: ₹450.
Quick-commerce handling fee: ₹25.
Rain surge charge on baby formula: ₹60.

Your mother says: Humne toh dabba dabba doodh nahi khareeda.

You are paying a surge price to keep a toddler quiet.
accepted.caption: Every diaper change has an associated platform fee.

accepted.trend: Baby Care Quick-Commerce Startup Kiddo, Raises Pre-seed Round of 12.5 Cr Led by Campus Fund
accepted.context: People in their late 20s and early 30s are deciding if they can afford families while staring at tech-fueled inflation.
accepted.angle: Startups can raise crores in minutes based on baby data, but you can't get a raise to actually pay for the baby.
slides: There are two financial models running your house.

One is a startup raising ₹12.5 crore to deliver baby wipes on a bike.
The other is you calculating if you can afford play school on a single salary.

The startup got funded in six weeks.

Your appraisal is in March.
accepted.caption: The VC market is bullish on babies. Your bank account is not.

accepted.trend: Indian Office Leasing Shifts to Connectivity and Air Quality
accepted.context: Tech parks and corporates are spending massive capital to upgrade physical offices so workers feel guilty about demanding remote work.
accepted.angle: Your office is becoming a highly sanitized, air-filtered luxury resort to mask the fact that you still live in a cramped flat next to a construction site.
slides: Your company's new office has hospital-grade air filtration.

The office: PM 2.5 levels at zero. Air circulated every six minutes. Leased line backup.
Your home: Rent up by 15%. Balcony covered in metro dust. Wi-Fi dropping twice during standup.

They built a perfect biosphere to keep you in desk 14.

You still cannot afford a balcony.
accepted.caption: Fresh air is now a corporate benefit. 💨
